Read the plan first: /Users/vaibhaav/.ao/data/artifacts/neatlogs-hack-1/tally-implementation-plan.md, especially "The routing rule" in section 3 and the feature tables in section 2. Spike findings from lane A appear in /Users/vaibhaav/.ao/data/artifacts/neatlogs-hack-1/spike-findings.md as they are completed; check it before relying on any outside tool.

BASE: The shared schema lives on the local branch ao/neatlogs-hack-2/root (lane A; also on origin once pushed). Start your branch from it: `git merge ao/neatlogs-hack-2/root` before writing anything. Read schema/types.ts and schema/fixtures/ first. If you need a schema change, do not edit schema/ yourself: message me (the orchestrator) with the exact change.

YOU OWN agent/ ONLY. Lane A owns engine/, cli/, adapters/, schema/. Lane C owns dashboard/, demo/. Stay out of those.

BUILD, test-first, in this order:
1. agent/ports.ts: the interfaces the CFO agent needs from the outside world, so lane A can implement them and you can test with fakes: sizing signals for a task (files touched, dependents, tests present), price history lookup (pass rate and average cost per task size and tier), budget remaining, live usage for a running session (tokens, estimated cost), stop a session, get a handoff summary for a failed session, call an LLM.
2. Sizer: turns signals plus the issue text into small / medium / large and a confidence score. Deterministic rules first; an optional LLM call may refine it.
3. Routing rule: pick the tier for a task. Send to a cheaper tier only when (cheap ceiling + P(cheap fails) x top cost) < top cost AND confidence is high enough; otherwise go straight to a stronger tier. The cheap ceiling defaults to 20% of the estimated top-tier cost for that task. Respect the budget remaining: never start a task whose ceiling does not fit. Tiers come from tally.yaml; never hard-code model names or the demo repo. Output a one-sentence plain-English reason for every decision (it is shown on the dashboard).
4. History: update pass rate and average cost per (task size, tier) after every attempt, with a sensible prior so the first run works with no history.
5. Ceiling watcher: given the live-usage port, decide when a running attempt has crossed its ceiling and must be stopped.
6. Escalation: after a failed or stopped attempt, choose the next tier up, at most one escalation per task, only if budget allows, carrying the handoff summary. Record handoff type per the schema.
7. Baseline mode: every task to the top tier, no ceilings, for the before/after comparison.
8. Tracing: wrap each CFO decision in a neatlogs trace once spike S3 says how; until then put tracing behind a port with a no-op default.

The LLM, where used, is reached through the port. The real implementation will call a LiteLLM gateway (OpenAI-compatible; LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL_IDS in ~/.tally/.env). Use a cheap model for sizing. Never print, log or commit secret values.

Every rule above needs unit tests with fakes, including: cheap chosen when confident, strong chosen when unsure, nothing started when budget is too small, stop at ceiling, one escalation only, baseline ignores routing.

PUBLISHING IS AUTHORISED: push your branch to origin (Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack) and open PRs against main, one per coherent piece, small commits. Do not create plan or analysis documents in the repo. Report with `ao report` at each milestone and faithfully, including failures.

# Tally: implementation plan

Written 10 Oct 2026, 16:00 IST. Submission closes 12 Oct, 23:55 IST (about 56 hours).

Tally is a CFO for a fleet of coding agents. You give it a backlog and a budget. It sizes each task, gives it to the cheapest model likely to finish it, stops any task that overruns its ceiling, hands failed work to a stronger model, and ends with a ledger tying every dollar to a merged PR.

Nothing in this document is built yet. Command names are proposals.

## 1. What the judges score, and what earns it

| Criterion | Weight | What Tally must show |
|---|---|---|
| The agent | 30% | A full run on a real backlog: plan, route, execute, verify, recover, finish. Measured against a baseline. |
| Use of neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai | 25% | Each product makes a decision possible at runtime, not just during the build. |
| Demo video | 20% | The dashboard tells the story: a routing decision, a stopped runaway, an escalation, the ledger. |
| Building in public | 15% | Posts tagged #neatHack through the build, using dashboard screenshots and real numbers. |
| Usefulness and originality | 10% | "They cap people, we cap tasks", backed by the Uber, Meta and Gartner evidence. |

Evidence the submission needs: two sets of neatlogs traces with compared numbers, a run where an action failed and what happened next, Entire checkpoints or entire-graph output, a cfo.ai business plan (pricing, costs, revenue, runway), a public repo with commits dated in the hackathon, and #neatHack links.

## 2. Features

### V1: the loop works end to end (target: 11 Oct, 14:00 IST)

| # | Feature | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Backlog intake | Reads GitHub issues with a label; a YAML file is the fallback and the rerun format. |
| 2 | Task sizing | Runs entire-graph on each task to estimate files touched and dependents, and labels it small, medium or large. |
| 3 | CFO agent | An LLM agent that picks a model per task from the size, a price table and the budget left, and writes its reason in one sentence. |
| 4 | Fleet execution | Spawns one Agent Orchestrator worker per task with the chosen model, in its own branch. |
| 5 | Verification | A task passes only if the repo's tests pass for that task. The agent's own claim is not accepted. |
| 6 | Per-task spend ceiling | Each task gets a ceiling from its size. A watcher stops the worker when it is crossed. |
| 7 | Escalation | A failed or stopped task goes to the next model up, once, if budget allows. |
| 8 | Ledger | One row per attempt: task, size, model, tokens, cost, result, PR link. Saved as JSON. |
| 9 | Live dashboard | Budget bar, task rows with the decision sentence, and the ledger. Runs locally. |
| 10 | Tracing | Every CFO-agent decision and every worker run is traced in neatlogs from the first run. |
| 11 | Dry-run mode | Fake workers with scripted outcomes, costing nothing, so the loop and dashboard can be tested freely. |

### Final: everything furnished (target: 12 Oct, 12:00 IST)

| # | Feature | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| 12 | Routing from history | The CFO agent uses real cost and pass rate per task size and model from earlier runs, replacing the static price table. |
| 13 | Handoff, not restart | Escalation passes the Entire handoff summary and the saved branch, so the stronger model continues the work. |
| 14 | Live budget in cfo.ai | Budget is read from a cfo.ai scenario; actual cost is written back after each task. |
| 15 | Baseline mode | `--baseline` sends every task to the top model, for the before/after comparison. |
| 16 | Experiment report | Runs each mode more than once and reports cost per merged PR, pass rate and spread. |
| 17 | Trace and checkpoint links | Every dashboard row links to its neatlogs trace, Entire checkpoint and PR. |
| 18 | Hosted dashboard | Public URL on AWS showing the recorded final runs. |
| 19 | Market list | CrustData search for engineering teams adopting coding agents, feeding market size into the plan. |
| 20 | Business plan | cfo.ai model with pricing, costs, revenue and runway. |
| 21 | Budget-low alert | One Slack webhook message when a run ends or budget drops below a threshold. Cut first if time is short. |

### Usable by a judge on their own repo (part of Final)

Tally drives coding agents on the user's own machine, so it is installed, not hosted. A judge gets three ways in, from no effort to full use:

| # | Way in | What it needs | What they see |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22 | Hosted dashboard | A browser | Our recorded runs: the ledger, the decisions, links to traces and checkpoints. Read-only. |
| 23 | `tally demo` | Node only. No accounts, no keys. | The full loop with simulated workers on a sample backlog, in the live dashboard. About two minutes. |
| 24 | `tally init` in their repo | Agent Orchestrator, plus whichever of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai they have | Tally running their agents on their issues. |

What makes way 24 work:

| # | Feature | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 25 | Setup wizard (`tally init`) | Detects the repo's test command, asks for a budget and an issue label, and connects each product in turn: neatlogs key, `entire enable`, the cfo.ai login. Writes `tally.yaml`. |
| 26 | Health check (`tally doctor`) | One line per product: connected, missing, or broken, with the exact command to fix it. |
| 27 | Config file (`tally.yaml`) | Test command, model tiers with their harness and list price, ceilings, budget source. Any harness Agent Orchestrator supports can be a tier. |
| 28 | Each product optional | Without cfo.ai the budget is a number in the config. Without neatlogs, history is local only. Without Entire, sizing falls back to code search and escalation restarts. The dashboard shows which are off. |
| 29 | Quickstart in the README | Install to first run in under ten commands, with the three ways in at the top. |

This costs roughly half a day of lane A and lane C time. The engine must therefore never hard-code the demo repo: repo, test command and tiers come from config from the first commit.

### Deliberately out
Logins, multi-user support, creating tasks in a browser, a Slack bot, a hosted service that runs agents on someone else's repo, and more than one escalation step.

## 3. How it fits together

```
GitHub issues ──▶ Intake ──▶ Sizer (entire-graph) ──▶ CFO agent ──▶ AO worker (chosen model)
                                                        ▲   ▲              │
                              price history (neatlogs) ─┘   │              ▼
                              budget left (cfo.ai) ─────────┘         Verifier (tests)
                                                                     │            │
                                                                  passed        failed / over ceiling
                                                                     │            │
                                        cost ──▶ ledger ──▶ cfo.ai   ◀┘            ▼
                                                    │                 Entire handoff ──▶ stronger model
                                                    ▼
                                                dashboard
```

Parts, each with one job:

- **Engine**: the run loop and state. Owns the ledger file.
- **Adapters**: one thin module per outside tool (Agent Orchestrator, Entire, neatlogs, cfo.ai, GitHub). The engine never calls a tool directly, so a tool that misbehaves can be swapped for its fallback.
- **CFO agent**: the only place an LLM makes a spending decision.
- **Watcher**: polls each running worker's token use and enforces the ceiling.
- **Dashboard**: a static page that reads the ledger and run state. It never writes.
- **Demo target**: `Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev` (Python, 16 test files run with `make test`), with the backlog filed as issues on it. Collaborators' repos can be added later as further targets.

Stack: TypeScript on Node for the engine, adapters and CLI; a static HTML and JS dashboard with no framework; JSON files for state.

Model tiers come from `tally.yaml`. The main set is the seven models on the LiteLLM gateway, cheapest first: nova-micro, nova-lite, nova-2-lite, nova-pro, claude-haiku, claude-sonnet-4.6, claude-opus-4.6. These are paid per token, so the ledger can show real spend. Whether each can drive a coding worker under Agent Orchestrator is spike S7; any that cannot are still usable for the CFO agent's own sizing and routing calls. The Claude Code subscription models (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, set through `ao spawn --model`) are the fallback set. Codex models are also available through `ao spawn --harness codex`; they slot into the same tiers once their list prices are confirmed, and a Claude Code to Codex escalation is the cross-agent handoff Entire documents.

### The routing rule, and why a failed cheap attempt cannot sink the run

The CFO agent sends a task to the cheap model only when the expected cost is lower than going straight to the top model:

    cheap ceiling + P(cheap fails) x top cost  <  top cost

Three things keep this true in practice:

1. **The cheap attempt is capped.** Its ceiling is set as a fraction of what the top model would cost for that task (default 20%). So the most a wrong guess can add to any task is 20%, and that worst case is known before the run starts.
2. **Only confident tasks go cheap.** The sizer scores each task (files touched, dependents, whether tests already exist for the area, how specific the issue is). Tasks the CFO agent is unsure about go to the middle or top model directly.
3. **It learns.** Every result updates the failure rate for that task size and model. If cheap keeps failing on a class of task, the rule stops sending that class there.

Handoff lowers the cost further, because the stronger model starts from the failed attempt's branch and summary instead of from nothing.

With a 20% cap, the cheap route breaks even when it fails about 80% of the time. Whether real failure rates sit below that on this backlog is what the experiment measures.

Cost is always tokens used multiplied by published list price. That keeps numbers comparable whether a worker runs on an API key or a subscription.

## 4. Unknowns to settle first (spikes, 16:30–19:30 IST today)

Each has a fallback so nothing here can block V1.

| # | Question | Fallback if the answer is no |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Can a script spawn an AO worker with a chosen model, read its status and result, and kill it? | `--model` exists on `ao spawn`. If status is hard to read, poll the worker's branch and PR instead. |
| S2 | Can token use for a running worker be read while it runs? | **Settled, yes.** The AO daemon serves `GET /api/v1/usage/sessions/{sessionId}` on localhost, returning live token totals and an estimated cost per session and per model for Claude Code and Codex. Checked against the running daemon on 10 Oct. The watcher polls this. |
| S3 | Does neatlogs expose past run cost and outcome through an API? | Tally keeps its own history file built from the same data; neatlogs remains the trace record and the evidence. |
| S4 | Does entire-graph give usable impact numbers from the CLI on a fresh repo? | Size tasks by counting files matched by a code search on the issue text. |
| S5 | Does the Entire handoff summary work when the next agent uses a different model? | Pass the failed session's summary from `entire checkpoint explain` plus the branch. |
| S6 | Can an agent write a value into a cfo.ai scenario through the MCP server after one browser login? | Tally writes a CSV that is imported into cfo.ai after each run. |

## 5. Work split

At most three AO workers run at any time, in three lanes. Each lane owns its own folders, so lanes do not edit the same files. The ledger and event schema is the first thing merged, because every other part reads it.

| Lane | Owns | Order of work |
|---|---|---|
| A: Engine | `engine/`, `cli/`, `adapters/` | Spikes S1–S6, then schema, run loop, ledger, dry-run mode, then the adapters (AO, Entire, GitHub, neatlogs, cfo.ai), then baseline mode and the experiment runner. |
| B: CFO agent | `agent/` | Sizer, routing rule, ceilings and the watcher, escalation and handoff, neatlogs tracing, history-based routing. |
| C: Dashboard and demo | `dashboard/`, `demo/` | Dashboard against dry-run data, the backlog of issues on the target repo, trace and checkpoint links, AWS hosting. |

Each piece of work is also a GitHub issue on the Tally repo, so human contributors can pick up an issue instead of an AO worker. A lane has one owner at a time, human or agent.

Each worker's PR gets AO's native review before merge.

## 6. Timeline (IST)

| When | Milestone | Proof |
|---|---|---|
| 10 Oct 16:30–19:30 | Spikes done; schema agreed; Entire enabled on the repo; target repo chosen. | Findings note. |
| 10 Oct 19:30–11 Oct 02:00 | Engine, dashboard and CFO agent working in dry-run mode. | Dry run shows a routed, failed, escalated and passed task on the dashboard. |
| 11 Oct 02:00–14:00 | **V1**: real workers on the demo backlog, traced in neatlogs. | One full real run with a ledger. First neatlogs traces. |
| 11 Oct 14:00–22:00 | History routing, Entire handoff, cfo.ai read and write, links. | A forced-failure run showing handoff. cfo.ai scenario updated by the agent. |
| 11 Oct 22:00–12 Oct 08:00 | Experiment: baseline runs and Tally runs. | Comparison report from neatlogs traces. |
| 12 Oct 08:00–12:00 | **Final**: hosted dashboard, CrustData list, business plan. Feature freeze at 12:00. | Public URL. Plan in cfo.ai. |
| 12 Oct 12:00–19:00 | Record and edit the demo video; finish hackathon.md and evidence links. | Video file. |
| 12 Oct 19:00–22:00 | Submit. Three hours of slack before the 23:55 cutoff. | Submission confirmation. |

If the plan slips, cut in this order: Slack alert, AWS hosting (show the dashboard locally), third repeat of each run, live cfo.ai write (use the CSV fallback). Never cut the forced-failure run or the baseline comparison; both are named evidence.

## 7. The experiment

- **Backlog**: 7 tasks on the demo target: 3 small, 3 medium, 1 that looks medium but is hard.
- **Before**: every task on the top model, no ceilings.
- **After**: the same tasks routed by Tally.
- **Repeats**: 2 of each, 3 if time allows. One run each proves nothing, because token use on identical tasks can vary widely.
- **Reported**: cost per merged PR, pass rate, total cost, and the spread across repeats. Every run is published, including any where Tally loses.
- **Reset**: each run starts from the same commit of the demo target.

Tally never runs more than 3 workers at once. The experiment is 7 tasks x 2 modes x 2 repeats = 28 task runs in total, taken three at a time, one after another. At roughly 10 to 15 minutes a task that is about two to three hours. A third repeat adds 14 more runs and is done only if time allows.

## 8. How you test it

Tests are ordered from cheapest to most expensive. Do not move to the next level until the current one passes.

| # | Test | How | Pass when |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Unit tests | `npm test` | Routing picks the expected model for each size and budget; ceiling maths and ledger totals are right. |
| T2 | Dry run | `tally run --dry-run --budget 40` | Dashboard shows all 7 tasks routed, one failing and escalating, the budget bar ending at the ledger total. Costs nothing. |
| T3 | One real task | `tally run --only <issue> --budget 5` | A worker opens a PR, tests pass, one ledger row appears, a trace appears in neatlogs, a checkpoint appears in Entire. |
| T4 | Forced failure | Run one medium task with a ceiling set far too low. | The worker is stopped at the ceiling, the ledger shows a stopped attempt, a stronger model picks up the same branch and finishes. This is the recovery evidence. |
| T5 | Budget too small | `tally run --budget 2` | Tally completes what it can, marks the rest "not started: no budget", and total cost stays under the budget. |
| T6 | Bad task | Include one issue that cannot be solved. | It fails on both models, is marked failed, and the run still finishes the other tasks. |
| T7 | Interrupted run | Kill Tally mid-run, then start it again. | It resumes from the ledger without redoing finished tasks or double-counting cost. |
| T8 | Full run | `tally run --budget 40` on all 7. | Every task is passed, failed or skipped with a reason; ledger total equals the sum of rows and matches cfo.ai. |
| T9 | Comparison | `tally experiment --repeats 2` | The report shows both modes with spread, and every number can be traced to a neatlogs trace. |
| T10 | Stranger install | A teammate who has not seen the code follows only the README on their own machine and repo. | `tally demo` works with no accounts; `tally doctor` names every missing piece correctly; `tally init` then `tally run` completes one task on a second repo. |
| T11 | Missing products | Run with each of neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai switched off in turn. | The run still completes, and the dashboard says which product is off. |

### Evidence check, one per product
- **neatlogs**: open a trace for a CFO decision and one for a failed worker; the failure point is visible.
- **Entire**: `entire checkpoint list` shows checkpoints for worker sessions; the handoff summary for the T4 task exists.
- **cfo.ai**: the budget scenario shows a value the agent wrote; the business plan page exists and is shareable.
- **CrustData**: the search that produced the market list can be rerun and returns the same kind of results.
- **Repo**: commits are dated 10–12 Oct and the repo is public (it is now).

## 9. What only you can do

Already in place (checked 10 Oct): GitHub CLI logged in, Entire CLI logged in, the Tally repo is public.

Keys go in one file, `~/.tally/.env`, outside every repo so it cannot be committed and every worker can read it:

| Name | For | Needed by |
|---|---|---|
| `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` | Sending traces, reading run history | First real run |
| `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY` | Market list | Final |
| `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_REGION=us-east-1` | Hosting the dashboard | Final. The AWS CLI also needs installing. |
| `SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL` | Optional alert | Only if the alert is built |

Two things need a browser and cannot be done by an agent:

- **cfo.ai**: run `claude mcp add --scope user --transport http cfoai https://api.cfo.ai/mcp`, then approve in the browser while logged in to cfo.ai. Until this is done Tally uses the CSV fallback, so nothing is blocked.
- **cfo.ai model skeleton**: budget, actuals, pricing, revenue and runway, so the agent has cells to write into.

Also yours: choosing the target repo for the backlog, posting the #neatHack updates, recording the video.

## 10. Risks

- **Routing may save less than hoped.** The routing rule in section 3 caps the loss from a wrong guess at 20% per task, so the downside is bounded. The size of the saving is still unknown until the experiment runs, and the result is published either way.
- **No Anthropic API key.** Workers and the CFO agent run on the Claude Code (Pro) and Codex subscriptions. Cost in the ledger is AO's estimated cost at list price, not money actually billed, and the video must say so. Pro-plan usage limits may pause workers mid-run, especially on the top model; Codex models are the relief.
- **The target repo's tests are unverified.** `fly-doom-jev` has a pytest suite, but it needs Python 3.14, a native kernel build and possibly large data files. Whether the tests run cleanly in a fresh worker checkout is the first thing to check. It has no open issues, so the backlog has to be written.
- **The failure scene may not happen naturally.** A prepared scenario (T4, a ceiling set too low on one task) produces it, and the video says that is what was done.
- **Sizing may misjudge tasks.** A task that looks small but is not will fail on the cheap model. The cap limits the cost, and the backlog includes one such task on purpose.

# Sample tally.yaml for the finished-run fixture.
# The repository, test command and tiers below are examples; Tally reads all
# of them from this file and assumes nothing about the target repository.
version: 1

repo:
  path: .
  slug: acme/payments-service
  baseBranch: main

test:
  setupCommand: npm ci
  command: npm test
  timeoutSec: 900

backlog:
  source: github-issues
  issueLabel: tally

# Ordered from cheapest to strongest. Escalation moves one step right.
# price is the published list price in USD per million tokens; check it
# against the provider's pricing page before a real run.
# ceilingFraction is the share of the size ceiling a tier may spend.

    harness: claude-code
    model: claude-haiku-4-5-20251001

git push -q -u origin ao/neatlogs-hack-5/routing 2>&1 | tail -3; gh pr create --base main --head ao/neatlogs-hack-5/routing --title "CFO agent: ports, sizer, price history and the routing rule" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

First piece of lane B (`agent/` only).

- `agent/ports.ts`: the interfaces the CFO agent needs from outside: sizing signals, price history, budget remaining, live usage, stop a session, handoff summary, LLM, tracing. Lane A implements them; `agent/testing/fakes.ts` has in-memory versions for tests and dry runs.
- `agent/sizer.ts`: files touched, dependents, tests present and the issue text become small / medium / large plus a confidence score. Rules are deterministic. An optional LLM call (through the port) can raise confidence when it agrees; when it disagrees the larger size wins and confidence drops, so the LLM alone can never make a task cheaper.
- `agent/history.ts`: pass rate and average cost per (size, tier), updated after every attempt, with a prior worth two attempts so the first run works with no data. `PriceHistory.snapshot()` is plain JSON for the engine to save.
- `agent/router.ts`: a cheaper tier is chosen only when `ceiling + P(fails) x top cost < top cost` and confidence is high enough; otherwise a stronger tier. Nothing starts unless its ceiling fits the budget left. Every decision carries a one-sentence reason. Tiers, prices and ceilings come from `tally.yaml`; no model or repo names in code.

## Depends on

Built on #1 (schema and scaffold). Until #1 merges this diff also shows its commits; the lane B changes are everything under `agent/`.

## Tests

`npm test` (58 agent tests pass) and `npm run typecheck`. Covered: cheap chosen when confident, strong chosen when unsure, the break-even maths, learning from repeated failures, nothing started when the budget is too small, ceiling never above budget left, tiers by any name and count, history or signals port failing.

## Known limits and follow-ups

- Prior pass rates and sizing thresholds are guesses until the experiment gives real numbers.
- Watcher, escalation, baseline mode and tracing follow in the next PRs.
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2
